definition: Panegyric means a formal speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word panegyric. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know panegyric should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The stadium program opens with a panegyric for the club's oldest season-ticket holder — sixty years of loyalty recounted without one word of reproach.
Plain praise is the everyday material — a kind word at any volume — and it stops far short of a panegyric, which builds praise into formal architecture.
A toast is warmer and more public than a stray kind word, but it stops short of a panegyric: one raised glass and a minute of affection, not an hour of organized glory.

An encomium is a composed, formal piece of glowing praise — a panegyric's nearest twin, and like a panegyric it is a deliberate production rather than a passing remark. Where the two differ is scale: an encomium can live comfortably in a page, while a panegyric builds the full public monument, delivered at length.

A eulogy is formal praise for someone who has died, delivered at a funeral or memorial. A panegyric is every bit as formal, but its subject is typically alive to blush — often seated in the front row. If the honoree can hear it, panegyric is the word.

You already know pan- from panorama and pandemic, but the root egyr- ('assembly') reached English inside this single word and died out everywhere else. Nothing to peel and reuse — remember the festival crowd instead: all of Greece, gathered to hear somebody praised.
Panegyric means a formal speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly.

Panegyric is more precise than 'speech' or 'tribute' because it names praise at full volume and full length — formal, public, and unmixed with criticism.
A toast admires for thirty seconds; a panegyric builds its subject a monument out of sentences.
